To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the highly indebted countries are not in a position to repay their debts; (2) the adjustment policies followed by them have been highly recessive; (3) the resumption of growth requires a major restructuring of the external debt and a major restructuring of trade policies.
the adjustment policies of the 1980s have been largely unsuccessful in restoring growth and reducing debt in the highly indebted developing countries.
the debt crisis has had a negative effect on growth and on the standard of living of the poor in highly indebted countries.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether and how trade liberalization can contribute to economic recovery in the debt-ridden countries.
the impact on growth and employment of structural reforms in highly indebted countries, particularly the developing ones.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the structural adjustment in the debt ridden countries has been inadequate, slow, and highly recessive.
the adjustment policies followed by the highly indebted countries have not been adequate to secure sustained growth.
the debt crisis has been a major economic and social disaster for the highly indebted countries.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is a strong case for the highly indebted countries to undertake trade reforms.
trade reform is a necessary condition for growth, but not sufficient.
the debt crisis has been a serious setback for the highly indebted countries and has been accompanied by a sharp decline in living standards.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the adjustment policies of the past decade have been too restrictive and have failed to generate sustained growth.
the adjustment policies of highly indebted countries have not only been highly recessive but also highly inequitable.
trade liberalization is not a panacea for highly indebted countries, especially when it is not accompanied by a sound macroeconomic framework.
